text:
I’ll model the water as the annular rotating passage between the solid hub (`r=12 mm`) and outlet (`r=58 mm`), from the backplate flow face at `z=4 mm` to the shroud at `z=18 mm`. The axial inlet is the annulus `12–16 mm` at the top; this resolves “hub bore” as the axial eye around the hub, since a literal bore through the stated solid hub would terminate at the backplate. The seven blades occupy `r=16–58 mm`, follow a 30° backward sweep, and will be subtracted from this water volume.

I’ll generate the boundary directly as named triangulated patches and use `cartesianMesh`, first at a coarse nominal 4 mm background size. A 2 mm root fillet is below that coarse cell scale, so I’ll omit it as explicitly permitted; that also avoids creating under-resolved sliver cells. First I’m plotting the exact blade planform and measuring its sweep and thickness.

The planform is consistent: seven passages remain separated, blade thickness is constant, and the trailing edges reach the 58 mm radial outlet. I’ll now make the coarse 3D water volume. I’m retaining a topological split at the 16 mm eye radius solely so the axial inlet and shroud can receive distinct names; it is an internal conformal interface, not a wall. Boundary faces are identified by their originating analytic surfaces (top eye plane, top outer plane, bottom plane, hub cylinder, outlet cylinder, or blade-cut surface).

The CAD boolean succeeded, but my first outlet classifier assumed OCC would report a cylinder’s center of mass on its axis; for a full cylindrical sheet OCC instead reports a point on the sheet. I’ll inspect the actual analytic surface metadata before rebuilding, rather than guessing the outlet tag.

The inspection shows why the first topology was unnecessarily fragmented: overlapping the already-existing eye shell created duplicate sliver faces. I’m rebuilding cleanly as one eye volume plus seven outer passage volumes sharing a conformal interface. This preserves the inlet/shroud split without duplicate geometry. Cylindrical outlet arcs are distinguished from blade cuts by their native OCC cylinder type and large centroid radius; the blade sides remain spline surfaces and their radial end caps remain planes.

I’m re-emitting the successful coarse build with its own `gmsh` and `math` imports so it is reproducible in `build.py`. The reported “no tetrahedra” entities are zero-volume OCC bookkeeping remnants from the conformal fragment, not failed water regions; the actual eight fluid subregions (eye plus seven passages) contain 12,417 tetrahedra. I’ll filter those remnants during the final reproducible build by retaining only positive-volume entities.

The mesh itself has 12,417 valid tetrahedra and no ill-shaped tetrahedra after Gmsh optimization. I’ll now convert that coarse mesh to OpenFOAM and inspect the actual patch table and topology; this is the decisive test for whether the OCC bookkeeping warnings affected the exported cells.

All six requested patches survived conversion with nonzero face counts. The conversion warnings are unmatched duplicate interface triangles from the redundant OCC entities; they were not used as OpenFOAM boundary faces. I’ll run `checkMesh` now to determine whether the retained volume is conformal and connected, and then render the actual OpenFOAM mesh rather than relying on CAD alone.

`checkMesh` did not yet inspect geometry because this OpenFOAM build requires placeholder `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries even for mesh checking. I’ll add empty valid dictionaries and rerun; this does not define a solver or boundary conditions.
This installation also validates the standard scheme subdictionaries on startup. I’ll provide minimal `none` entries and rerun the same mesh-only check.

The coarse OpenFOAM mesh is one connected region, closed, correctly scaled, and has acceptable aspect ratio, non-orthogonality, and skewness. The two extended-check failures are: 84 unused Gmsh bookkeeping points and OpenFOAM’s determinant metric on tetrahedra (a known stringent extended metric; cell volumes and face tets are valid). I’ll remove the unused points by subsetting the complete `water` cell set, then rerun both standard and extended checks.

After removing unused points, the standard binding check reports **Mesh OK**. The sole extended warning is the tetrahedral determinant heuristic; there are no negative/zero-volume cells, face-tet errors, openness errors, or topology errors, so I will retain this valid coarse mesh rather than refine a geometry the user asked to begin coarsely.

Now I’ll render the actual OpenFOAM mesh surface, with the inlet and outlet highlighted, to verify the axial eye, curved passages, and radial discharge visually.

`subsetMesh` wrote the cleaned mesh at time `0` while leaving the original in `constant`; `foamToVTK` therefore exposed that it had rendered the uncleaned copy. I’ll promote the cleaned mesh to `constant/polyMesh` and remove the transient mesh directory, ensuring downstream OpenFOAM utilities all use the same checked mesh.

The canonical mesh now passes standard `checkMesh` with one region, 12,417 cells, six named patches, closed boundary, and correct metre-scale bounds. I’ll make the final visual inspection from that canonical mesh, using translucent backplate/shroud so the blade passages remain visible.

The render revealed one dimensional interpretation worth correcting before finalization: the blades/shroud are 14 mm above the backplate flow face, but the specified hub rises 18 mm. I will therefore extend the axial eye and hub 4 mm above the shroud, placing the inlet at `z=22 mm` while retaining blade tips/shroud at `z=18 mm`. This both honors the separate 18 mm hub rise and gives a short axial approach before the water turns into the passages. The exposed `r=16 mm` eye casing between 18 and 22 mm will be part of the shroud patch.

The corrected CAD measures `18 mm` hub rise (`z=4–22 mm`) and `14 mm` blade/shroud rise (`z=4–18 mm`), with all six patch groups present. I’ll replace the prior mesh, remove any conversion-only unused points as before, and run the final canonical check.

The extended-eye mesh passes, but its maximum aspect ratio (138) and 11 severe non-orthogonal faces expose slivers caused by the artificial radial fragment interface. I won’t accept that avoidable quality loss. I’ll rebuild the same geometry as a single Boolean fluid volume: the full lower annulus minus blades, fused to only the 4 mm axial eye extension. This removes the artificial internal interface while preserving the inlet and shroud as separate boundary faces.

The clean Boolean now contains only the expected eight positive volumes (central eye plus seven blade-to-blade passages), with no duplicate OCC regions. I’ll convert and check this improved candidate, replacing the prior canonical mesh only after conversion.

The clean topology reduces the worst aspect ratio from 138 to 71 and remains one connected region with `Mesh OK`, but I’ll make one final quality pass using Gmsh’s Netgen tetrahedral optimizer on the existing mesh. This changes node placement/connectivity only, not geometry or patch identities.

The optimizer preserves the same accepted quality: 12,164 tetrahedra, one connected region, valid positive volumes, and standard `checkMesh: Mesh OK`. I’ll refresh the final image from the corrected 22 mm-high canonical mesh and then finish.

Completed the centrifugal-impeller water mesh:

- 7 blades, measured 3.000 mm thick.
- Blade centerline sweep measured −30.000° from 16 to 58 mm radius.
- Blade/shroud passage height measured 14.000 mm.
- Hub radius 12 mm and rise 18 mm above the backplate flow face.
- Axial inlet is the 12–16 mm annulus at `z=22 mm`; radial outlet is at 58 mm.
- Backplate solid radius/thickness represented by its requested 60 mm support and flow face at `z=4 mm`; only the water passage to 58 mm is meshed.
- Separate patches: `inlet`, `radial_outlet`, `blades`, `backplate`, `hub`, `shroud`.
- Final mesh: 12,164 tetrahedra, one connected water region, SI metres.
- Standard `checkMesh`: **Mesh OK**.

Assumptions/omissions: rotation was taken as positive counter-clockwise, with blades swept 30° in the opposite direction. The inlet was interpreted as the annular eye around the solid hub. The requested 2 mm blade-root fillets were removed because the chosen coarse nominal 4 mm cell size cannot resolve them. The mesh passes the binding check, although its coarse transition near the 4 mm eye extension has maximum non-orthogonality 85.97° and aspect ratio 70.98; both remain within this `checkMesh` acceptance.
